analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement against paying women less than men for comparable work.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 31 Senate cosponsors and a 2000 committee hearing but never got a markup or a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the Equal Pay Act by making it easier for women to win back wages lost to sex discrimination: it narrows the excuses employers can use to justify pay gaps, lets workers sue as a class, allows compensatory and punitive damages, and protects employees who discuss their wages from retaliation. It would also require the EEOC to start collecting pay data by sex, race, and national origin, and create voluntary tools and awards for employers who fix their own pay gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men for work requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility. They would gain stronger legal remedies — back pay plus compensatory and punitive damages, class-action rights, and expert fees paid by the losing employer — and an easier path in court, because employers could only justify pay gaps with factors that are genuinely job-related or serve a legitimate business purpose [S2] [S3]. Job applicants would be covered, and the equal pay rule would apply across an employer's operations rather than one facility at a time [S3]. Workers who ask about or share wage information could not be fired or punished for it [S2] [S3]. Employers who already pay fairly could win recognition and technical help evaluating their pay scales [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women paid less than male coworkers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the stakes for paying women less: employers found in violation would owe back pay plus compensatory or punitive damages, and workers could sue as a class and recover expert witness fees — remedies the Equal Pay Act today does not provide

Makes it harder to justify a pay gap: an employer relying on education, training, or experience would have to prove the factor is job-related or serves a legitimate business purpose, was applied reasonably, and is not itself the result of discrimination
Extends the equal pay rule beyond a single facility — so a woman could compare her pay across an employer's operations, not just her own establishment — and covers job applicants
Protects workers from retaliation for asking about, discussing, or disclosing wages, which is a practical precondition for ever finding out you are underpaid
Requires the EEOC to issue regulations collecting employer pay data by employees' sex, race, and national origin, giving enforcement agencies the information needed to spot discrimination patterns

Directs the Labor Department to train enforcement staff, publish research, convene a national summit, offer voluntary job-evaluation guidelines, and recognize employers who close gender pay gaps without cutting men's wages

analysis.who_pays: Employers that are not paying equal wages. They would face back pay liability with compensatory and punitive damages, expanded class-action exposure across their establishments, legal costs including experts' fees, new EEOC pay-data reporting, and compliance costs from tightened legal defenses. Employers already in compliance would bear only modest reporting and paperwork burdens. The federal government would fund new training, research, and award programs, with appropriations authorized at whatever sums are necessary [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers found to pay women unequally

drawbacks.text: The compliance and litigation burden on employers is real: unlimited punitive damages, class actions, expert fees, and the removal of the 'within any establishment' limit could expose companies to claims comparing pay across facilities in very different local labor markets

Defenders of current law argue pay differences often reflect experience, seniority, or market factors; the bill narrows employers' ability to raise those defenses by requiring the factor to be job-related, reasonably applied, and not itself discriminatory

The bill is mostly remedies and paperwork — training, studies, a summit, and a medal — rather than a direct wage increase, so its actual effect on the gender pay gap depends entirely on litigation and enforcement that individual workers would have to initiate
It authorizes appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, leaving taxpayers on the hook for an open-ended new federal data-collection and outreach effort

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For working women facing genuine discrimination, the bill offers meaningful new remedies and practical tools — wage transparency, class actions, and real damages — that current law lacks. The costs fall mostly on employers who would be found in violation, and the bill deliberately preserves employer defenses (bona fide factors, no requirement to cut men's pay) to blunt the harshest objections. The trade-off is heavier litigation exposure for businesses and some compliance costs, but the bill's larger weakness is design, not fairness: much of it is studies, awards, and voluntary guidelines that would have done little on their own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee, which held one hearing but never voted to send it to the floor, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Tom Daschle introduced the bill on January 19, 1999 with 23 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
The cosponsor list grew to 31 senators, every one a Democrat; no Republican ever signed on
The committee took no action for over a year, then held a single hearing on June 8, 2000 (printed as S.Hrg. 106-631) — the only substantive step the bill ever received
The committee never reported the bill out and the full Senate never debated or voted on it; it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with sex-based pay gaps are better off: they kept the weaker remedies and narrower enforcement of the existing Equal Pay Act, with no punitive damages, no class actions, no cross-establishment comparisons, and no federal pay-data reporting.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the cosponsor coalition

for.name: 31 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Ted Kennedy and John Kerry, but could not get it out of committee

for.name: Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on June 8, 2000, printed as S.Hrg. 106-631

against.name: Jim Jeffords
against.role: Chairman, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; over two years it was never given a markup or a vote, only a single hearing

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 31 cosponsors was a Republican, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action beyond a hearing

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored the bill; the Republican-run HELP committee never moved it past a hearing, so the bill died without a single floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Employers with sex-based pay gaps would face punitive and compensatory damages, nationwide class actions, expert fees, and new EEOC pay-data reporting. The bill's benefit to workers is precisely a cost to them, so their interest ran against it.

The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs would have to train staff and affected contractors on wage-discrimination enforcement, adding compliance obligations but also clearer guidance on equal-pay expectations.
